name: Gambia
summary_text: Same-sex conduct has been criminalised in Gambia since historic-era rule, retained from the 1933 Criminal Code implemented in 1934 as carnal knowledge against the order of nature. Section 158 previously punished homosexual acts by up to 14 years imprisonment for men and women, after the Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 2005 extended gross indecency to women. The Criminal Code (Amendment) Act signed in October 2014 created aggravated homosexuality carrying mandatory life imprisonment for serial offenders, for gay or lesbian people living with HIV, for acts with persons under 18, with disabled or drugged persons, or where the accused was a parent, guardian or authority figure. That life clause was removed by the Criminal Code adopted in March 2025, which instead imposes a five-year minimum sentence for unnatural offences defined in statute as any homosexual act with no stated maximum, and three years for gross indecency.  Gender expression is separately restricted. Since 2013 section 167 of the Criminal Code forbids men to dress as women, punishable by up to five years imprisonment or a fine of 50,000 Gambian dalasi. Gambia makes no provision for official change of gender and citizens cannot change legal gender. No law or regulation protects residents against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.  Same-sex couples have no legal recognition in Gambia. LGBTQ people are prohibited from adopting children.  Enforcement under the current framework is active. The Barrow government has not typically enforced the provisions and promised not to prosecute same-sex couples for consensual sexual acts, while stating there are no plans for liberalisation. The United States Department of State reported arrests and societal discrimination in 2020 and no prosecutions but continued stigma and police harassment in 2021. On 5 March 2026 the Brusubi Magistrates Court sentenced Muhammad Jawo and Muhammad Krubally each to five years imprisonment for violation of section 147(1) for indecent conduct between men in an unfinished building.  Foreign visitors have been directly targeted under these laws. On 15 May 2008 President Yahya Jammeh gave homosexuals 24 hours to leave the country and ordered the Inspector General of Police and the director of the Gambia Immigration Department to conduct mass patrols, warning that any hotel, lodge or motel lodging such persons would be closed. He also vowed to cut off the head of any homosexual and threatened dismissal of gay soldiers. In June 2008 two Spanish men in their 50s alleged to be gay were arrested and detained at Kotu police station after taxi drivers reported them, and were released after intervention by the Spanish government. On 23 December 2008 Frank Boers, a 79-year-old Dutch national, was arrested at Banjul International Airport when officials found pornography including nude photos of himself and Gambian men in his possession, and was convicted of indecency and fined 100,000 dalasis in lieu of a two-year sentence.  Gender non-conformity has been policed. Human Rights Watch reports regular organised actions by law enforcement against persons suspected of gender non-conformity. On 10 April 2012 police arrested 18 men at a bar in the Tourism Development Area, 16 Senegalese, one Gambian and one Nigerian, for indecent practice after testifying the men were wearing women's clothes, carrying handbags and walking like ladies. A court remanded the men and the prosecutor dropped all charges on 1 August 2012. In November 2014 state forces launched an investigation under the aggravated law producing at least eight arrests, including at least four adult men, a 17-year-old boy and nine women, with three more men interrogated in December 2014. Detainees were held at the National Intelligence Agency headquarters in Banjul and allegedly tortured and ill-treated to compel confessions. Arrests are believed to have been common during the Jammeh presidency, though data is lacking.  Societal risk remains severe. A 2021 to 2023 survey found 93 percent of Gambians would dislike or strongly dislike having a homosexual neighbour. The media promotes misinformation and harmful stereotypes toward LGBTQ people. There are no LGBTQ organizations in the country after 2016 because it is considered too dangerous, which leaves visitors without local support structures. In 2023 there were reports of healthcare workers refusing to honour LGBTQ people's privacy, which negatively impacted HIV care for LGBTQ Gambians. The 2014 life sentence for gay or lesbian people living with HIV created a direct barrier to testing and treatment.

name: Guatemala
summary_text: Private consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults has been lawful in Guatemala since 1871.  Guatemala provides no legal gender recognition for trans people. Since 2016 a person may change a legal name to match gender identity only with judicial permission. Legal gender cannot be changed. A person cannot self-report gender for official documents, which must show the sex and name assigned at birth. The resulting mismatch between appearance and identity documents exposes trans visitors to scrutiny during identity checks.  Guatemala is bound by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights advisory opinion of 9 January 2018, OC-24/17, which holds that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a human right under the American Convention on Human Rights and which requires access to marriage and all existing family registration systems for same-sex couples. Guatemala was among the countries urged in January 2018 to comply. Compliance has not been recorded.  A December 2017 bill that would have recognized the right to gender identity and permitted change of name and gender on birth certificates was rejected in August 2018 by the Legislative and Constitutional Points Commission and the Women's Commission. A later proposal for a gender identity law to allow correction of official documents was advocated but was not enacted. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2022 on legislative attacks including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.  Vociferous opposition defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against legal gender recognition in Guatemala.  Guatemalan law prohibits no discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, health care, banking or public accommodations including cafes, restaurants, nightclubs and cinemas. A May 2017 bill to add gender identity to Criminal Code articles 27 and 202 as a protected category was not adopted.  No hate-crime protection covers gender identity. Bias-motivated crimes on that basis are reported to be tolerated by the Government, particularly harassment and violence directed at transgender people. The lack of protection is attributed to prevailing attitudes about sexual identity and gender roles.  Guatemalan officials have excluded trans women from femicide protections on the stated ground that transgender women are not biological women. Central American governments have long maintained that exclusion. The exclusion is official and shapes the violence risk for trans women in Guatemala.  Trans women held in custody are placed according to birth sex in the men's prison system, a practice documented as of 2020. Placement in men's prisons facilitates anti-trans violence and exposes trans women to sexual assault. Trans activist Barbara Herrarte of Red Multicultural de Mujeres Trans described repeated forced sex at night by other detainees while held in a men's prison.  United Nations and non-governmental reports from the late 1990s documented systematic lethal targeting of LGBT people as part of a social cleansing campaign. That record includes the 1997 shooting in Guatemala City of transgender AIDS activist Luis Palencia.  Guatemala grants no legal recognition to same-sex couples through marriage, civil unions or domestic partnership. A civil unions bill introduced in December 2016 by Deputy Sandra Moran has not been debated since. Lawmakers responded to the Inter-American Court opinion with Initiative 5272, the Protection of Life and Family Act, to explicitly ban same-sex marriage, define family as a father, a mother and children, increase penalties for abortion, provide that freedom of conscience and expression protects refusal to accept non-heterosexual conduct as normal, and describe homosexuality as contrary to biology and genetics. The initiative passed first and second readings but its third reading was blocked in September 2018 with no debate since. A renewed congressional approval of Law 5272 on 9 March 2022 to ban same-sex marriage and punish abortion with 5 years in prison was archived and discarded on 15 March after President Alejandro Giammattei announced a veto as violating the Constitution and international agreements.  Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender people from schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from gender identity disorders and to require censorship of media including transgender people. The Education, Science and Technology Committee of Congress approved it unanimously and sent it for full congressional review.

sources.documents: Holds parties to the American Convention on Human Rights should grant same-sex couples access to all family registration including marriage, and that recognition of gender identity on official documents is a human right protected by the Convention; article states Guatemala is legally bound by it

Bill 5490 advanced in December 2021 to remove education regarding transgender people from schools on grounds of protecting children and adolescents from gender identity disorders and to require censorship of media including transgender people. The Education, Science and Technology Committee of Congress approved it unanimously and sent it for full congressional review.
